To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intravenous challenge of mice with fibrillar prion strains can generate novel prion strains with altered biochemical, biological and pathological properties.
prion‐containing blood can generate novel prion conformers in the brain, and that these novel conformers may be generated in the spleen.
prions that do not normally invade the central nervous system can do so after being introduced into the body via blood transfusion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the conformation of prions impacts brain entry and how prions may be transmitted via transfusion.
the generation of novel neuroinvasion phenotypes from prion strains that do not normally invade the CNS, and how this may be relevant for prion diseases in humans.
how prions spread and replicate in the body, and the potential for prions to generate new disease phenotypes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
intravenous prion challenge can lead to the generation of a new prion strain, which is neuroinvasive and which can cause disease.

the fibrillar mule deer prion strain (mCWD) is not neuroinvasive, however, when introduced to the brain via intravenous challenge, the prion strain can change to a novel strain, which is highly neuroinvasive.
intravenous prion challenge can generate novel neuroinvasiveness, which may arise from prion replication or selection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

intravenous exposure of a prion‐containing blood product may lead to the generation of new prion conformers in the brain, and that the new prion conformer may have a different disease outcome than the original strain.
prion conformers are not static, and that prions are capable of generating new conformers that may have altered neuroinvasion and disease properties.
intravenous prion challenge generates novel neuroinvasive conformers that may arise from prion replication and/or conformer selection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intravenous prion transmission may generate novel prion strains and that the prion strain generated may be dependent upon the conformation of the prion inoculum and the route of inoculation.
prions can be generated from non‐neuroinvading prions following intravascular exposure, which may have important implications for prion disease transmission.
the neuroinvasiveness of a prion strain is a function of its conformational properties and that the brain is not the only site where prions can replicate.
